In 1778 Thomas Malthus predicted that population growth would outpace food production to the point that the people of Europe would have to endure shortages and starvation. This catastrophe was no sooner proposed than the industrial revolution increased agricultural productivity to levels never thence imagined, allowing us to produce globally more than enough food to feed all 7+ billions eaters on this planet. That people still starve is attributable to a number of other factors, but not at all to the overall ability of the planet to sustain us, which is Malthus feared.

I have seen the 21st-century technological bottleneck referred to as the "new Malthusian trap". The argument there is not, of course, that people will starve because we haven't colonized the moon, or mastered cold fusion, or any other such Kardashev scale advancements. Rather, it recognizes that the inability to reap the cascading benefits afforded by Moore's Law, or alternatively the diminishing returns therefrom (either reality bears the same consequences) portends a future where we fall prey to, if not hunger, then some other environmental or biological reality we are ill-equipped to face. It was technology that thwarted the hunger trap, and it will be technology that thwarts the disease trap, or the climate trap (the real one, not the lefty made-up one), or the meteor trap, or the exploding sun trap. Eventually we will come up against one of these walls, and if we cannot scale it we will be left to molder in the dust bin of history with all those other extinct species.
